0.comment: Melanta: Temple of Space and its decree
0.content: In The Wind Has Ceased, Istoria explains that the Temple of Space selects people and objects from a single age or vanished civilisation and keeps them as living memories. It was probably not designed as an eternal paradise. The God of Space's sisters (the other Shades) occasionally brought things in and granted small pardons for acts of change. Melanta, driven by longing for his creator, reversed all of this and began purging anything that had changed.

1.content: Melanta's punishments fit the sin he saw: residents of the Mahavaipulya Chamber who wrote their own novels, blurring fact and fiction, were turned into pages; residents of Luyang Academy were pressed into ink blots in paintings; those in the Desert Pavilion were turned to sand. The painter "Maukie" (Escher) was exiled for defiling the laws of space. The Traveler and Zeitlind undo these in the quest series.

2.content:
Climbing to the Atrium of Suchness requires giving up memories: they become the stairway through the Corridor of Nothingness. Raumhilda gave hers and Melanta broke half the corridor in rage. In The Final Judgment Zeitlind offers hers, and they intertwine with her sister's, so the path stands again and the Traveler can reach him. Istoria says the Corridor draws its power from the temple itself and that the Watchers exist to uphold its rule of departure.

Istoria calls the last glimpse of the world an act of mercy, unconnected to passing the Corridor. After the battle Zeitlind returns below and does not remember the party.

3.content: After defeat he says that when the divine leaves the throne all creations are free. He admits that exiling the painter and severing the path were transgressions that triggered his self-destruction, calls his deeds an attempt to correct others, and confesses jealousy of Nihilita, of change, freedom and life. He tells the Traveler to find their sibling themselves, tells Zeitlind about the knights who fell on Windrest Peak, and ends with words for Nihilita: his weariness runs deeper than words.
